title: A limiter that rejects instead of queueing

blocks.text: For rate limiting the page advises `tryAcquire()` **without blocking**: reject the excess work instead of queueing it. Two of its pitfalls apply at once: release the permit in `finally`, or one exception leaks it for ever; and only release what you acquired, or the count inflates beyond its limit.
Write `Bulkhead`, which lets at most `limit` tasks run at the same time:

items: `<T> Optional<T> tryCall(Supplier<T> task)` runs `task` if a slot is free **right now** and returns its result; if every slot is busy it returns `Optional.empty()` at once, without waiting at all (not even a short timed wait) and without running the task. Whatever the task throws, an exception or an `Error`, reaches the caller, and the slot is given back either way.
`int available()` is the number of free slots.

blocks.text: A caller whose interrupt flag is set is not refused for that: with a slot free, its task runs. The tests never race two callers for the last slot, so doing the check and the take as one atomic step, which is why the page uses `tryAcquire()`, is good practice they do not grade.

rows: `Optional.empty` at once; the task did not run
a call was rejected while another ran; that one finished

cases.says: With a slot free, the task runs, its result comes back, and the slot is free again.
With every slot busy, a call is rejected at once, without waiting even briefly, with an empty result, and its task does not run.
A task that throws, an exception or an Error, passes it on and still gives its slot back.
A rejected call gives back no permit, so the limit is not inflated.
The slot is taken with a check that never waits: a caller whose interrupt flag is set still gets a free slot, where any wait, even a timed one, would throw InterruptedException first.

concepts: For rate limiting, tryAcquire() without a timeout rejects excess work at once instead of queueing it.
A permit is released in a finally block, so an exception in the guarded work cannot leak it.
A call that failed to get a permit must not release one, or the limit grows with every rejection.
